messages.subject: Standardized significant, unstandardized not
parts:
OK, I'm sure this has been explained--and recently--but I wasn't paying attention. I estimate a model from Anderson and Narus (1984)--attached are a covariance matrix (string), model syntax, and a transcript. The unstandardized results and the standardized results don't seem to match. Here is a piece of the unstandardized parameters:

  outcl =~                                            
    x5                1.000                           
    x6                7.828    5.602    1.397    0.162

and here are the standardized estimates:

5     outcl =~       x5   0.469 0.177   2.651  0.008
6     outcl =~       x6   0.822 0.291   2.826  0.005

I don't understand how the standardized estimates are highly significant, when the unstandardized loading for x6 is not.

Also, can someone point me to the documentation where it explains the source of the standard error for the standardized version of the loading that was fixed to 1?

Again, I am sure this has been discussed recently, but I can't put my hands on it now.. Thank you.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Standardized significant, unstandardized not
parts:
On 10/05/2016 03:34 AM, Edward Rigdon wrote:
> Can I make a second appeal for a pointer toan explanation for these results?

There seem to be two things:

1) why is the standardized loading significant, while the unstandardized
loading is not (or vice versa): the sampling behavior of an
unstandardized parameter is different from the sampling behavior or a
standardized parameter. The latter is a function of three quantities:
the factor loading and two variances: the factor variance and the item
(residual) variance: all of them vary from sample to sample!

2) the 'fixed' factor loading is no longer 'fixed' in the standardized
case, because it is a function of the factor variance and the item
(residual) variance, which vary from sample to sample, and therefore,
the standardized factor loading varies from sample to sample...

Yves.
